title: Date published: May 24, 2026 How to Use Critical Chain Methodology in Engineering Teams
author: Ojstersek, Gregor
summary: This guest post from Gregor Ojstersek's Engineering Leadership newsletter features Senior Engineering Manager Karol Wojciszko's case study on applying an adapted version of Goldratt's Critical Chain project management methodology to software engineering teams. The core mechanic is counter-intuitive: all individual task estimates are cut by 50% to create 'aggressive but achievable' targets, and the removed time is pooled into a shared project buffer rather than hoarded in individual task padding. The method addresses a fundamental pathology in engineering project management: Parkinson's Law — work expands to fill available time. Traditional estimates embed safety padding, but that padding is consumed by the very conditions it is meant to protect against (late starts, scope creep, meetings, interruptions). By removing padding from individual tasks and pooling it, Critical Chain makes the project's true scheduling risk visible and shared, rather than hidden in optimistic individual estimates. Wojciszko's implementation uses a simple traffic-light gauge that tracks the ratio of buffer consumption to project progress, updated weekly by pulling completed tasks from Jira. Green means the project is finishing ahead of buffer use and no action is needed. Yellow means alignment is roughly maintained and only trend-watching is required. Red means buffer is being consumed faster than progress is being made and a 30-minute retrospective is warranted. The entire weekly management overhead is about 10 minutes. The article is direct about failure conditions: Critical Chain does not work with junior-heavy teams (who take aggressive estimates personally and experience anxiety regardless of assurances), with unclear scope, or in team cultures that lack the professional maturity to distinguish between aggressive scheduling and unfair pressure. In the right environment, Wojciszko reports projects completing 20-30% ahead of historical median delivery time.
points: Goldratt's insight is that engineers, like most workers, embed safety padding into individual estimates and Parkinson's Law ensures the work expands to fill that time; Critical Chain addresses this by cutting estimates 50% and pooling the saved time into a shared project buffer that the whole team draws from as needed.

The gauge-based tracking system (green/yellow/red based on buffer consumption vs. project progress) converts a complex project management question into a single weekly visual judgment, dramatically reducing the cognitive overhead and ceremony of oversight without sacrificing signal quality.

The method works precisely because it removes stigma from individual task overruns: no one is punished for using the buffer, and team attention shifts from individual performance to collective project health — a cultural change that makes honest estimation and honest reporting possible.

Critical chain fails with junior-heavy teams, who take 50%-cut estimates personally and experience anxiety even when no penalties are attached; the method requires a team culture that can clearly distinguish between ambitious scheduling and unfair pressure.

The practical outcome in the case study: projects completing 20-30% ahead of historical median delivery time, achieved primarily by surfacing Parkinson's Law padding that had previously expanded unnoticed to fill allotted time.
quotes: The core mechanic in critical chain project management is almost provocatively simple. You take your team's estimates, cut them all by 50%, and call these new numbers 'aggressive but achievable.' The time you removed from each task doesn't disappear. It becomes your project buffer: a shared pool of time that the entire team draws from.

My entire engagement with this method during a project looked like this: Refresh the data (I pulled the completed tasks from Jira into the spreadsheet). Look at the gauge chart: Green: I'm done for the week. Yellow: I note the trend, and then I'm done for the week. Red: I schedule a 30-minute retro. That's it. No daily tracking, no manual data entry, no complex dashboards.

I've tried this, and it backfired. Juniors take the aggressive estimates personally. Even when I explicitly say 'no penalties,' even when I demonstrate it with my behavior, they stress about missing the target. It creates anxiety instead of motivation. The method requires a certain level of professional maturity to work.

Red = buffer consumption exceeds progress by more than 5 percentage points above the historical median. At this pace, you'll blow through the buffer before completing the scope. Time to act - call a retro, find the constraint, fix it.
Individual padding, which had previously quietly expanded to fill their allotted time now generate actual savings for the project.
Once set up, the method runs on 10 minutes of your time per week. The team does nothing extra. No additional tracking, no extra ceremonies, no new tools to learn.
